title: ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation

Photograph: Panama Landscapes by Oyvind Martinsen/Alamy Southern frontlines: Latin America and the Caribbean Panama ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive Supported by About this content Jessica Rawnsley in Panama Tue 20 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 07.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze. In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama ’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves. Delgado’s milk production has fallen by half. As the dry season approaches, he is selling off cattle for fear of what is to come. He says: “I and other producers have had to slaughter or sell animals of high genetic value simply to avoid the heartbreaking prospect of watching them die of thirst or starvation. The lack of water has greatly affected us, and it is going to continue to do so.” Panama is gripped by a water crisis. A rainy season punctuated by drought, exacerbated by the climate crisis, has ravaged large swathes of the country. El Niño threatens to continue the havoc. In August, the government declared a national state of emergency that will remain in place until June 2027. Authorities forecast rainfall deficits of more than 50% in some regions until December. View image in fullscreen A farmer crosses the Indio River on his horse at Tres Hermanas community, one of the towns threatened by the reservoir project. Photograph: Enea Lebrun/Reuters “The situation is dramatic,” says Panama’s environment minister, Juan Navarro. “Climate change has undoubtedly increased the frequency and also the gravity of El Niño, as well as other climate extremes; we used to get an El Niño every 10 or 20 years. The last, in 2023, cost the Panama canal almost a billion dollars in revenue.” How the climate crisis threatens the Panama Canal – and the country’s future Read more And this latest El Niño, Navarro says, citing scientists, is pointing towards being the worst in history . He says: “We are already starting to feel the impact, but we have seen nothing yet. For Panama, this is life or death. The canal is life and death for our economy, and for our drinking water supply.” Panama’s economy relies heavily on the Panama canal – and the canal is acutely vulnerable to the climate crisis. The 50-mile (80km) waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, through which about 5% of global maritime trade flows , accounts for up to 7.7% of Panama’s GDP . The freshwater lakes that supply the canal’s locks, Gatún and Alajuela, also provide drinking water for about 2 million people – nearly half of Panama’s population . A sizeable chunk of the country’s hydroelectricity generation also depends on the watershed. In September, low water levels twice triggered restrictions on daily vessel transits. While some have been lifted, officials are braced for worse when the El Niño-intensified dry season begins in December. View image in fullscreen Ships in the Panama canal in September 2023, waiting for the congestion caused by intense droughts in the country to pass. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images The government is funnelling $80m (£60m) towards “resilience actions” to prepare for El Niño, Navarro says. In the long term, it is investing about $1.5bn in a reservoir on the Indio River intended to supply Lake Gatún and meet demand for the next five decades.
